HOW ONLINE FRAUDS WORK
What is it?

An online fraud is a trick that uses a phone, app, website or message to make a person give away money, details or access. Almost every fraud is social engineering: it targets feelings — fear, greed, urgency, trust or kindness — rather than technology. Once you know the pattern, you can spot a scam you have never seen before.
Why money disappears so fast

UPI and IMPS move money in seconds, at any hour. Fraudsters pass it through several mule accounts — accounts rented or opened in other people's names — and withdraw it as cash or crypto. Reporting on 1930 lets banks place a hold on money still in those accounts; every minute of delay lets more of it leave.
Phishing: fake messages and websites
What is it?

Phishing is a fake message, email or website that pretends to come from a trusted organisation — a bank, electricity company, courier, tax department or employer — to steal login details, card numbers or OTPs, or to make you install a harmful app. Smishing is phishing by SMS; vishing is by voice call.

Sunita received an SMS saying her bank reward points would expire today. The link opened a page that looked exactly like her bank. She entered her customer ID, password and then the OTP. Within minutes, ₹48,000 was transferred out. Lesson: the page address ended in a different domain, and the bank's real app would never ask for an OTP to “redeem points”. Never open a bank, tax or utility service from a link in a message. Type the address yourself or use the official app.
UPI, QR code and OTP frauds
What is it?

UPI is safe when you understand one rule: the UPI PIN authorises money to leave your account. Fraudsters invent stories that make you enter it while believing you will receive money — a refund, a prize, an advance payment or a “wrong transfer” to return.

Arjun listed his old sofa online. A “buyer” said he was being transferred and would send ₹10,000 in advance. He sent a QR code and said, “Scan and enter your PIN to receive.” ₹10,000 left Arjun's account. The “buyer” said it was a mistake and asked him to try again. Lesson: you never scan a code or enter a PIN to receive money. Stop at the first request.
Shopkeepers: protect your QR
Check the sound-box or app alert for every payment; never trust a customer's phone screen.
Check periodically that the QR sticker at your counter has not been covered with a fraudster's sticker.
Use separate UPI IDs or accounts for business and savings, and set daily limits.
Receiving money needs nothing from you. PIN, QR scan or OTP to “receive” = fraud, every time.
Fake bank, KYC and customer-care frauds
What is it?

The caller says your KYC has expired, your card will be blocked, or you have a pending reward. Or you search online for a company's helpline and call a fake number placed by fraudsters. Either way, the “executive” asks for card details or OTP, or asks you to install a screen-sharing or remote-access app so they can “help”. RBI and banks repeatedly warn: no bank employee will ask for your PIN, OTP, CVV or password, or ask you to install a remote-access app. KYC is updated through the branch, the official app or the official website.

Job, investment and "digital arrest" scams
What is it?

These scams use greed or fear. Task-based job scams pay small amounts for liking videos or rating hotels, then demand ever-larger “investments”. Investment scams add victims to WhatsApp or Telegram “stock tips” groups and fake trading apps showing false profits. In a digital arrest scam, callers pose as police, CBI, customs or narcotics officers on video and keep the victim on camera until money is paid.

Kavya earned ₹150 for liking three videos and was moved to a Telegram group of “earners”. Over four days she paid ₹1.8 lakh in “merchant tasks”. Her dashboard showed ₹3 lakh, but withdrawal needed a 20% “tax”. Lesson: a job that asks you to pay is not a job.

Impersonation and recovery scams
What is it?

Fraudsters pretend to be someone you trust: a relative in trouble abroad, a friend whose WhatsApp has been taken over, a senior officer, a soldier buying your goods. New AI tools can clone a voice from a short clip. After a fraud, victims are often targeted again by fake recovery agents who promise to get the money back for a fee.

Mr Iyer received a call in his grandson's voice: “Dadu, I've had an accident, please send ₹50,000 to this number, don't tell Mum.” He paid. Later the grandson was found safe at college. Lesson: agree a family code word, and always call back on the number you already have.

Reporting and golden-hour response
What is it?

The golden hour is the first hour after a fraudulent transaction. A call to the 1930 helpline (run under the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, MHA) sends the details to banks and payment apps so they can try to hold the money before it leaves mule accounts. The complaint is then completed on cybercrime.gov.in (the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, NCRP).

Role of the First Responder

Do: stay calm; stop further payments; call 1930 with the victim; call the bank; save evidence; help file on NCRP; note every reference number and time; follow up. Never: ask for the victim's PIN, OTP or password; call or threaten the fraudster; promise the money will return; charge any fee; delete evidence.
